originalTitle: Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera

content: Lee Chang Dong’s seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff – 2,600 employees – after which many died by suicide. Possible Love is the latest in a long line of Lee movies that engage with themes of class or labor or religion or compressed modernity, that uniquely Korean affliction, without feeling didactic. A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go. The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English. I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education? As you know well, Daegu is referred to as the heartland of conservatism in Korea. I went to school there, all the way through university, so I grew up steeped in that conservative disposition and was influenced by it. But until I graduated from college, in the spring of 1980, I didn’t realize how politically conservative Daegu citizens were. That spring, in May of 1980, I participated in protests against the Chun Doo-hwan regime as a university student. It was on the streets that I met them, the citizens, and experienced their hardline sentiments in a visceral way. It was shocking to me. Afterwards, I thought a lot about how come the people in Daegu were so politically conservative. In light of all that, the thoughts of a person I perceive as myself, that person’s attitude towards the world, could only be bound with a certain kind of tension. I was interested in how different directors respond to similar social forces in different ways – like Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice. I imagine you know them both personally. What is the conversation between you all when working on your various projects? We do know each other personally, but we seldom talk about our work. It might be the result of coincidence. Though of course, there might be a certain inevitability hidden within them. We lived through the same modern Korean history, and you cannot call that coincidence. One thing does come to mind. A long time ago, I think before he made Mother, Bong Joon Ho told me over drinks that he had almost finished writing a script and wanted to show it to me. It was a story about a mother, and he was wrestling with how he could portray that person’s pain, whether he even had the right to. He said he wanted to show me the script. But once he sobered up, maybe he forgot, because he never showed it to me. Later, when I saw the film, I felt I might understand what he had been talking about. Possible Love is concerned with similar questions: How can I portray another person’s story, another person’s pain? What position am I in? How much distance should I keep from them? You could say that these questions around the ethics of the camera are connected to the worry Bong Joon Ho had back then. Like Ye-ji, I come from the so-called margins, and now report on that terrain, which is perhaps why watching her character pursue a near-vampiric level of access, I felt something close to repulsion. How were you able to represent the filmmaker–participant dynamic so accurately? I can’t say how accurate it is. I don’t think Ye-ji’s attitude can be generalized. Not every documentary filmmaker has a rich husband. Nevertheless you can say Ye-Ji captures something universal about filmmakers, or those who deal in other people’s stories, directors such as myself, or reporters, in that they aren’t exactly the people they portray. Even if they came from a lower class, they are no longer of it. Their position in life has changed. And yet, in order to do their work, what do they do? When someone else’s suffering unfolds dramatically in front of them, are they to capture the moment on tape, or should they step away from the camera? Or maybe it isn’t unfolding dramatically in front of them, in which case, do they create a certain effect by producing the moment, by staging it? [Image: What does it mean to capture someone on film? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Possible-Love_NYFF64_05.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] I think those are basically properties of the camera. The moment you hold a camera you have power, and the camera operates according to that power. It’s not so much that I portrayed it so precisely, but these properties of the camera are something worth thinking through together. For us filmmakers, we don’t belong to the world of our subjects, nor are we on the side of capital either. We are in the middle where we are, it can be said, in a neutral, or perhaps cowardly position. Despite that, those who make movies, those who tell stories of others, in the end, can, through their efforts, bring about some small change. In this film, Ho-seok ends up pouring out what’s inside of him in front of the camera, which functions as a kind of treatment, even if that isn’t what Ye-ji intended. Possible Love is a collaboration between you and screenwriter Oh Jung-mi. How did you two come to work together, and what does that collaboration look like? chineseContent: 李沧东的第七部长片《可能的爱》的灵感源自 2009 年的真实事件，当时一家韩国企业集团解雇了三分之一的员工（2,600 名员工），之后许多人自杀身亡。 《可能的爱》是李安一长串电影中的最新一部，这些电影涉及阶级、劳动、宗教或压缩现代性等主题，这是韩国特有的痛苦，但没有说教的感觉。一部不同类型的电影可能会捕捉到劳工斗争的激烈程度。 《可能的爱》在事件发生后与角色展开了对话，这是一个难以理解的阴暗时期。影片以一句铭文开头：“你不可贪图。”接下来是一部关于贪婪人物的电影。他们觊觎彼此的工作、名牌服装、配偶和地位。美玉（全度妍饰）是下岗丈夫浩锡（薛景求饰）长期受苦受难的妻子。在一位自杀身亡同事的葬礼上，美玉和浩锡遇到了另一对夫妇，即纪录片导演艺智（曹汝贞饰）和她富有的丈夫尚宇（赵寅成饰）。然后我们就出发了。 The Verge 在李前往纽约期间采访了他，谈论了他的政治观点、人与人之间的漏洞、摄像机的特性以及与 Netflix 合作的感受。采访以韩语进行，并翻译成英语。我也是大邱人。我想知道这个事实如何塑造了你？更广泛地说，你的政治教育归功于谁或什么？众所周知，大邱被称为韩国保守主义的中心地带。我在那里上学，一直读到大学，所以我从小就在那种保守的倾向中长大，并受到它的影响。但直到 1980 年春天我大学毕业时，我才意识到大邱市民在政治上是多么保守。那年春天，在
